topics.title: LR current growth
topics.idea: An inductor initially opposes the change of current; resistance sets the final DC value.
topics.result: $i=(V/R)(1-e^{-t/\tau_L})$, $\tau_L=L/R$, for i(0)=0 and a DC step V.
topics.explain: Kirchhoff gives $L\,di/dt+Ri=V$.::The source balances inductive and resistive drops.;;The final derivative is zero, giving $i_\infty=V/R$.::At steady DC there is no changing flux.;;The remaining distance to that final value decays exponentially with time L/R.::The first-order equation has a constant coefficient.;;At t=0, i=0 and $v_L=V$; at long time, $v_L=0$.::The current cannot jump but its derivative can.
topics.trap: Increasing R decreases the time constant and also decreases the final current at fixed V.
topics.check: At one LR time constant, what fraction of final current flows?=>$1-e^{-1}\simeq0.632$.

topics.title: LR current decay
topics.idea: After removing the source, an existing inductor current continues through the closed resistor path and dies away.
topics.explain: Choose the discharge loop so current initially retains its original direction.::Inductor current is continuous.;;Kirchhoff gives $L\,di/dt+Ri=0$.::There is no source supplying a rise.;;Solve with i(0)=I₀ to obtain exponential decay.::The derivative is proportional to negative current.;;Stored field energy becomes resistor heat.::An ideal inductor has no internal loss here.
topics.trap: Simply opening the current path can create a large voltage; the ideal decay formula assumes a closed R-L path.
topics.check: When current has fallen to half, what fraction of magnetic energy remains?=>One quarter.

topics.title: RC charging and discharging
topics.idea: A resistor limits how quickly a capacitor's voltage changes.
topics.explain: Use $Ri+q/C=V$ and $i=dq/dt$.::Kirchhoff plus charge storage gives a first-order equation.;;Initially an uncharged capacitor has zero voltage; after charging it holds the source voltage.::Capacitor voltage is continuous at switching.;;Remove the source into a closed R-C path and set the right side to zero.::Stored electric energy drives discharge.;;The negative discharge current means q decreases in the chosen capacitor-charge convention.::Current signs depend on the arrow definition.
topics.trap: Charge grows during charging while current decays; do not copy the same time dependence for both.
topics.check: At t=RC during charging, are q and i at the same fraction of their initial/final scales?=>No: q is 0.632 of final; i is 0.368 of initial.

topics.title: Free LC oscillations
topics.idea: An ideal capacitor and inductor swap electric and magnetic energy indefinitely.
topics.explain: Kirchhoff in the isolated loop gives $L\,di/dt+q/C=0$.::There is no resistor or source.;;Use i=dq/dt to get a second-order equation.::Capacitor charge is the state variable.;;At maximum charge current is zero; a quarter-cycle later charge is zero and current magnitude is greatest.::The energy moves between C and L.;;The sum $q^2/(2C)+Li^2/2$ stays constant.::There is no dissipative element.
topics.trap: An ideal LC circuit has no exponential decay. Real resistance makes the oscillation damped.
topics.check: When q=0 in a free LC oscillation, has all circuit energy vanished?=>No. It is stored in the inductor.

topics.title: LC response to a DC step
topics.idea: A constant source connected to an ideal LC series circuit does not create a settling exponential.
topics.result: For initially uncharged C and zero current: $q=CV(1-\cos\omega_0t)$, $i=CV\omega_0\sin\omega_0t$.
topics.explain: Write $L\ddot q+q/C=V$.::The source remains in the loop.;;Subtract the equilibrium charge CV: set x=q−CV.::This turns the equation into $\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=0$.;;Initial conditions are x(0)=−CV and $\dot x(0)=0$.::The capacitor was uncharged and the inductor carried no current.;;Solve to obtain q and i; capacitor voltage oscillates between 0 and 2V.::Without resistance there is no mechanism to settle.
topics.trap: This driven step response differs from free LC discharge; the source exchanges energy with the circuit.
topics.check: Does an ideal LC step current approach a nonzero constant?=>No. It oscillates about zero.

topics.title: Rotating-coil AC generator
topics.idea: Rotation changes flux linkage sinusoidally and produces an alternating emf.
topics.result: $\mathcal E=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, peak $\mathcal E_0=NBA\omega$, when the coil normal starts along B.
topics.explain: The linked flux is $NBA\cos\omega t$.::Area and field are fixed while orientation changes.;;Differentiate and apply Faraday's minus sign.::The emf is the negative flux-linkage rate.;;One complete rotation gives one sinusoidal cycle for this ideal two-pole geometry.::The orientation repeats after 2π radians.
topics.trap: Maximum flux occurs at zero emf; maximum emf occurs where flux crosses zero.
topics.check: If angular speed doubles, how do frequency and peak emf change?=>Both double.

topics.title: Pure R, L and C on AC
topics.idea: Resistance keeps voltage and current in phase; reactive elements shift them by a quarter-cycle.
topics.explain: For R, v=Ri, so their waveforms align.::No derivative or integral shifts phase.;;For L, $v=L\,di/dt$: voltage leads current by 90°.::A derivative advances sinusoidal phase.;;For C, $i=C\,dv/dt$: current leads voltage by 90°.::Here current is the derivative.;;Ideal L and C exchange energy with the source but have zero mean power.::Their instantaneous power alternates sign equally.
topics.trap: “ELI the ICE man”: in L, E leads I; in C, I leads E. State which quantity leads.
topics.check: What happens to capacitive reactance when frequency doubles?=>It halves.

topics.title: Complex impedance and series RL or RC
topics.idea: The j operator keeps magnitude and phase together during circuit addition.
topics.explain: Use the common current as phasor reference in a series circuit.::The same current passes through each element.;;Resistive voltage lies along I; inductive voltage is +90° and capacitive voltage −90°.::Use the pure-element phase laws.;;Add perpendicular components, then use Pythagoras for magnitude.::Voltages with different phases do not add as scalar magnitudes.;;The impedance angle is the voltage lead relative to current.::A positive angle means current lags the source.
topics.trap: Use j for the imaginary unit so i can denote current; phasors describe sinusoidal steady state at one frequency.
topics.check: A series RC circuit has negative impedance angle. Does current lead or lag?=>It leads source voltage.

topics.title: Parallel LC and antiresonance
topics.idea: Parallel branches share voltage; their reactive currents can cancel at the input.
topics.result: $Y=j(\omega C-1/(\omega L))$; at $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$, ideal input Y=0 and input impedance diverges.
topics.explain: Add branch currents $I_C=j\omega CV$ and $I_L=V/(j\omega L)$.::Parallel elements see the same phasor voltage.;;Factor V to identify admittance.::Current divided by voltage is Y.;;At resonance the imaginary contributions cancel.::The branch currents have equal magnitudes and opposite phases.;;The source current is zero although branch currents are not.::Current circulates between L and C.
topics.trap: This ideal parallel LC result differs from series resonance. Real coil resistance gives finite impedance and losses.
topics.check: At ideal parallel resonance, can inductor current be nonzero while source current is zero?=>Yes; capacitor current cancels it at the input.

topics.title: Series LCR and resonance
topics.idea: In series, L and C reactances cancel at resonance, leaving only R.
topics.result: $Z=R+j(\omega L-1/(\omega C))$; $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$; at resonance $I_{\rm rms}=V_{\rm rms}/R$.
topics.explain: Add the three impedances.::The same current flows through every element.;;Set the imaginary part to zero for resonance.::Voltage and current become in phase.;;Then impedance magnitude is minimum, R, and current is maximum for fixed source voltage.::The reactive contributions cancel as phasors.;;Individual L and C voltages can be large even though their sum vanishes.::Equal opposite phasors need not be individually small.
topics.trap: Below resonance the circuit is capacitive; above it the circuit is inductive.
topics.check: Does zero net reactance mean zero L and C voltages?=>No; their nonzero phasors cancel.

topics.title: Power in AC
topics.idea: Only the part of current in phase with voltage transfers net energy each cycle.
topics.result: $P=V_{\rm rms}I_{\rm rms}\cos\phi=I_{\rm rms}^2R$ for a series load with real resistance R.
topics.explain: Write $v=V_0\cos\omega t$ and $i=I_0\cos(\omega t-\phi)$.::Define positive φ as current lag.;;Multiply and apply the cosine product identity.::Separate a constant term from a double-frequency term.;;Average over a whole cycle.::The oscillating term integrates to zero.;;Replace peaks by rms values.::Each rms is peak divided by $\sqrt2$.
topics.trap: Apparent power VI in VA is not always real power in W. The power factor is cos φ.
topics.check: An ideal inductor draws rms current. Is its mean power necessarily positive?=>No. Its phase angle is 90°, so mean power is zero.

questions.prompt: Define the LR time constant, state its unit and explain its growth interpretation.
questions.answer: $\tau_L=L/R$ has units H/Ω = s. After one τ, initially zero current has risen to $1-e^{-1}=0.632$ of V/R. Equivalently the gap remaining to its final value is e⁻¹ of its original gap.
questions.final: $\tau_L=L/R$; 63.2% rise in one time constant.

questions.prompt: Why does current in an ideal inductor remain continuous when a finite DC voltage is suddenly applied?
questions.answer: The passive voltage is $v_L=L\,di/dt$. A finite voltage gives a finite slope, not an instantaneous finite jump. The initial current is therefore the pre-switch value even though the applied voltage changes abruptly.
questions.final: Finite inductor voltage implies continuous current.

questions.prompt: During LR decay, how much magnetic energy remains when the current is half its initial value?
questions.answer: $U_L=Li^2/2$. Therefore $U/U_0=(i/I_0)^2=(1/2)^2=1/4$. The remaining three quarters has been dissipated in the resistor for the ideal closed discharge path.
questions.final: 25% remains.

questions.prompt: Why must the LR decay formula specify a closed discharge path?
questions.answer: The formula solves $L\dot i+Ri=0$ with a finite resistor path. If a switch simply opens an inductor carrying current, a large voltage can develop to maintain continuity, potentially producing arcing. That situation is not the assumed ideal R-L loop.
questions.final: A defined resistor path is part of the exponential-decay model.

questions.prompt: An RC circuit has R=20 kΩ and C=50 μF. Find τ and the charging fraction at t=τ.
questions.answer: $\tau=RC=(2.0\times10^4)(50\times10^{-6})=1.0$ s. The capacitor voltage and charge reach $1-e^{-1}=0.632$ of their final values, while charging current falls to 0.368 of its initial value.
questions.final: τ=1.0 s; charge fraction 63.2%.

questions.prompt: Which capacitor quantity remains continuous under finite current at switching, and why?
questions.answer: Capacitor voltage remains continuous because $i=C\,dv_C/dt$. A finite instantaneous voltage jump would need an impulse of unbounded current in the ideal model. Charge q=Cv is likewise continuous.
questions.final: Finite current implies continuous capacitor voltage and charge.

questions.prompt: Write the natural angular frequency and frequency of an ideal LC circuit, and distinguish the units.
questions.answer: $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$ in rad/s, while $f_0=\omega_0/(2\pi)=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ in hertz. Confusing the two loses a factor of 2π.
questions.final: Angular frequency and ordinary frequency differ by 2π.

questions.prompt: An isolated LC circuit starts with a charged capacitor and zero current. Where is its energy after a quarter-cycle?
questions.answer: At $t=T/4$, $q=q_0\cos(\pi/2)=0$, so capacitor energy is zero. Current magnitude is maximal and all energy is magnetic, $Li^2/2=q_0^2/(2C)$.
questions.final: All stored energy is in the inductor.

questions.prompt: An uncharged capacitor and ideal inductor are connected in series to a DC source V at t=0. What is the maximum capacitor voltage?
questions.answer: $v_C=V(1-\cos\omega_0t)$ under zero initial current and charge. At half a natural period, cosine is −1 and $v_C=2V$. The ideal circuit does not settle because it lacks resistance.
questions.final: Maximum capacitor voltage is 2V.

questions.prompt: State the peak emf of a rotating N-turn coil and explain its dependence on angular speed.
questions.answer: For area A in uniform B, $\mathcal E_0=NBA\omega$. Faster rotation increases the rate of change of linked flux, so peak emf is proportional to ω. The result assumes rotation about an axis in the coil plane perpendicular to B.
questions.final: $\mathcal E_0=NBA\omega$.

questions.prompt: At what coil orientations are flux and emf maximum in an ideal AC generator?
questions.answer: Flux magnitude is maximum when the coil normal is parallel or antiparallel to B; its derivative and emf are then zero. Emf magnitude is maximum when the normal is perpendicular to B, where flux crosses zero fastest.
questions.final: Flux and emf maxima are separated by a quarter-cycle.

questions.prompt: Describe voltage, current and average power for a pure resistor driven by sinusoidal voltage.
questions.answer: Current is in phase with voltage because $i=v/R$. $I_{\rm rms}=V_{\rm rms}/R$ and $P=V_{\rm rms}I_{\rm rms}=I_{\rm rms}^2R$. Instantaneous power is nonnegative.
questions.final: A resistor dissipates positive mean power with power factor one.

questions.prompt: State the reactance and phase relation for an ideal inductor on sinusoidal AC.
questions.answer: $X_L=\omega L$ and $Z_L=j\omega L$. Voltage leads current by 90°, or current lags voltage by 90°. Average power is zero because stored magnetic energy is returned each cycle.
questions.final: Inductive current lags voltage by 90°.

questions.prompt: State the reactance and phase relation for an ideal capacitor on sinusoidal AC.
questions.answer: $X_C=1/(\omega C)$ as a positive magnitude and $Z_C=-jX_C$. Current leads voltage by 90° because $i=C\,dv/dt$. Mean power is zero for an ideal capacitor.
questions.final: Capacitive current leads voltage by 90°.

questions.prompt: What does multiplying a phasor by j do, and why is j used rather than i here?
questions.answer: Since $j^2=-1$, multiplication by j rotates a complex-plane vector +90° without changing its magnitude. The letter j avoids conflict with the time-dependent current i. It represents phase mathematically rather than a second physical current.
questions.final: j denotes a +90° phase rotation.

questions.prompt: Why can magnitudes of resistor and inductor voltages not be added directly in a series RL circuit?
questions.answer: They differ in phase by 90°. With current as reference, $\widetilde V=V_R+jV_L$, so $V=\sqrt{V_R^2+V_L^2}$, not $V_R+V_L$. Their instantaneous values still obey Kirchhoff's law.
questions.final: Add voltages as phasors, then take the magnitude.

questions.prompt: What are ideal input current and impedance at parallel LC resonance under an AC voltage source?
questions.answer: At $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$, $Y=j(\omega C-1/\omega L)=0$. Thus source current is zero and input impedance tends to infinity. Opposite nonzero branch currents can circulate.
questions.final: Ideal parallel resonance gives zero input current and infinite impedance.

questions.prompt: State the resonance condition and input impedance of a series LCR circuit.
questions.answer: Resonance occurs when $\omega L=1/(\omega C)$, giving $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$. Reactive impedances cancel, so Z=R, current is in phase with voltage and its amplitude is maximal at fixed V.
questions.final: At series resonance, Z=R.

questions.prompt: State whether a series LCR circuit is capacitive or inductive below and above its resonance frequency.
questions.answer: Below resonance, $1/(\omega C)>\omega L$, so net reactance is negative and current leads. Above resonance, $\omega L>1/(\omega C)$, so net reactance is positive and current lags.
questions.final: Below: capacitive. Above: inductive.

questions.prompt: Define power factor and distinguish real power from apparent power.
questions.answer: Power factor is $\cos\phi$, where φ is the phase difference of voltage and current for a sinusoidal load. Apparent power is $S_{\rm app}=V_{\rm rms}I_{\rm rms}$ in VA; real mean power is $P=S_{\rm app}\cos\phi$ in W.
questions.final: Only the in-phase contribution transfers net energy per cycle.

questions.prompt: Derive current growth in a series LR circuit connected to constant V at t=0, with i(0)=0.
questions.answer: Kirchhoff gives $L\dot i+Ri=V$.::Source voltage equals the two passive drops.;;Write $\dot i=(R/L)(V/R-i)$.::This exposes the final value and decay coefficient.;;The general solution is $i=V/R+Ke^{-Rt/L}$.::The deviation from the final value satisfies a decay equation.;;At t=0, $0=V/R+K$, so K=−V/R.::Apply the initial inductor current.;;Check i(0)=0, i(∞)=V/R and initial slope V/L.::All three physical limits agree.

questions.prompt: A 12 V step drives R=6 Ω and L=3 H from zero current. Find τ, i and inductor voltage at t=0.50 s.
questions.answer: $\tau=L/R=0.50$ s and $I_\infty=V/R=2$ A.::Determine time and current scales first.;;At one τ, $i=2(1-e^{-1})=1.264$ A.::Use the growth solution.;;$v_L=V-Ri=12-6(1.264)=4.415$ V.::The source voltage is shared between R and L.;;Equivalently $v_L=Ve^{-1}$.::The inductor's remaining drop decays exponentially.

questions.prompt: Derive LR decay from initial current I₀ and show the total resistor heat equals the initial magnetic energy.
questions.answer: $L\dot i+Ri=0$ gives $di/i=-(R/L)dt$.::No source remains in the closed loop.;;Integrate and impose i(0)=I₀: $i=I_0e^{-Rt/L}$.::The constant fixes the initial current.;;Heat is $W=\int_0^\infty Ri^2dt=RI_0^2\int_0^\infty e^{-2Rt/L}dt$.::Joule power is Ri².;;The integral equals L/(2R), giving $W=LI_0^2/2$.::The exponential vanishes at infinity.
questions.final: All initial magnetic energy becomes resistor heat: $W=LI_0^2/2$.

questions.prompt: An LR circuit has L=2 H and R=10 Ω. How long does current take to fall to 10% of its initial value?
questions.answer: $i/I_0=e^{-t/\tau}$ with $\tau=L/R=0.20$ s.::Use the current decay time, not the energy decay time.;;Set $0.10=e^{-t/0.20}$ and take logarithms: $\ln0.10=-t/0.20$.::A logarithm reverses the exponential.;;$t=0.20\ln10=0.4605$ s.::The negative log becomes a positive elapsed time.
questions.final: Current reaches 10% at about 0.461 s.

questions.prompt: Derive q(t), i(t) and capacitor voltage when an initially uncharged series RC circuit is connected to DC V.
questions.answer: $R\dot q+q/C=V$.::Use Kirchhoff and i=dq/dt.;;The final charge is CV and the time constant is RC.::Compare to the standard first-order equation.;;$q=CV(1-e^{-t/RC})$ meets q(0)=0.::The deviation from CV decays exponentially.;;Differentiate to get $i=(V/R)e^{-t/RC}$ and divide q by C for $v_C=V(1-e^{-t/RC})$.::Current is charge rate and voltage is charge per capacitance.;;Initially i=V/R while $v_C=0$; finally i=0 while $v_C=V$.::These limits check the solution.
questions.final: Charge and voltage grow; charging current decays.

questions.prompt: A 100 μF capacitor initially at 10 V discharges through 20 kΩ. Using i=dq/dt for its initially positive plate, find q, v and i after 2 s.
questions.answer: $\tau=RC=2$ s and $q_0=CV_0=1.0\times10^{-3}$ C.::Convert microfarads to farads.;;$q=q_0e^{-1}=3.679\times10^{-4}$ C and $v=10e^{-1}=3.679$ V.::The source-free charge decays.;;$i=-q_0e^{-1}/\tau=-1.839\times10^{-4}$ A.::The chosen positive plate loses charge.;;A current arrow in the discharge direction would instead have positive magnitude 0.1839 mA.::A negative sign describes the reference convention.

questions.prompt: For charging an initially uncharged capacitor from an ideal constant source V through R, find source work, final stored energy and resistor heat.
questions.answer: Total charge supplied is CV, so source work is $W_s=V\int i\,dt=V(CV)=CV^2$.::The source voltage stays constant throughout charging.;;Final stored energy is $U_C=CV^2/2$.::Capacitor energy is the integral of its rising voltage over charge.;;The difference $W_R=W_s-U_C=CV^2/2$ is resistor heat.::Energy is conserved.;;The result is independent of positive R, although R changes the charging duration.::A smaller R raises current but shortens the transient.
questions.final: Half the source energy is stored; half is dissipated in this ideal resistive charging process.

questions.prompt: An ideal isolated circuit has L=0.10 H, C=10 μF, initial capacitor voltage 20 V and zero current. Find q(t), i(t), frequency and peak current.
questions.answer: $q_0=CV_0=2.0\times10^{-4}$ C and $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=1000$ rad/s.::Use SI units in LC.;;$q=q_0\cos1000t$ and $i=-\omega_0q_0\sin1000t$.::Apply initial q and zero initial current.;;Thus $i=-0.20\sin1000t$ A.::Current is dq/dt.;;$f_0=1000/(2\pi)=159.15$ Hz.::Convert angular to ordinary frequency.
questions.final: $q=2.0\times10^{-4}\cos1000t$ C, $i=-0.20\sin1000t$ A; peak current 0.20 A.

questions.prompt: Derive the ideal series LC response to a DC step V with zero initial charge and current. Explain the voltage overshoot.
questions.answer: $L\ddot q+q/C=V$.::The source remains connected.;;Set x=q−CV to obtain $\ddot x+\omega_0^2x=0$.::The constant forcing shifts the centre of oscillation.;;Since x(0)=−CV and $\dot x(0)=0$, $x=-CV\cos\omega_0t$.::Use both initial conditions.;;Therefore $q=CV(1-\cos\omega_0t)$ and $i=CV\omega_0\sin\omega_0t$.::Differentiate charge for current.;;At $\omega_0t=\pi$, $v_C=2V$ and i=0.::The ideal inductor's stored energy and source work drive the overshoot.;;No resistor removes the oscillation energy.::The circuit does not settle in this ideal model.
questions.final: The capacitor voltage oscillates from 0 to 2V; this is distinct from free discharge.

questions.prompt: A 100-turn coil of area 0.020 m² rotates at 50 revolutions/s in a 0.10 T uniform field. Find angular speed, emf peak and rms emf.
questions.answer: $\omega=2\pi f=100\pi$ rad/s.::One revolution is 2π radians.;;$\mathcal E_0=NBA\omega=100(0.10)(0.020)(100\pi)=62.83$ V.::Differentiate the rotating flux linkage.;;$\mathcal E_{\rm rms}=\mathcal E_0/\sqrt2=44.43$ V.::The emf is sinusoidal.;;The electrical frequency here is 50 Hz.::This is the ideal two-pole geometry stated in the topic.
questions.final: ω=314.16 rad/s; peak emf 62.83 V; rms emf 44.43 V.

questions.prompt: Derive the impedances of an ideal inductor and capacitor using j and the common time factor $e^{j\omega t}$.
questions.answer: Differentiation of a sinusoidal phasor expression multiplies it by jω.::The derivative of $e^{j\omega t}$ is $j\omega e^{j\omega t}$.;;For L, $\widetilde V=j\omega L\widetilde I$, giving $Z_L=j\omega L$.::Use $v=L\,di/dt$.;;For C, $\widetilde I=j\omega C\widetilde V$, giving $Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)$.::Use $i=C\,dv/dt$ and $1/j=-j$.;;Their angles are +90° and −90° respectively.::Multiplication by ±j rotates the phasor.
questions.final: Inductive impedance is +jωL; capacitive impedance is −j/(ωC).

questions.prompt: At an angular frequency where $X_L=40$ Ω, a series RL circuit has R=30 Ω and source 100 V rms. Find Z, current, phase and real power.
questions.answer: $Z=30+j40$ Ω, so $\lvert Z\rvert=50$ Ω.::Series impedances add as complex numbers.;;$I_{\rm rms}=100/50=2$ A.::Use the magnitude form of Ohm's law.;;$\phi=\tan^{-1}(40/30)=53.13^\circ$; current lags.::The impedance angle is positive.;;$P=I^2R=120$ W, also $VI\cos\phi=100(2)(0.6)$.::Only R dissipates mean energy.
questions.final: Z=30+j40 Ω; I=2 A lagging 53.13°; P=120 W.

questions.prompt: A series RC circuit has R=60 Ω, $X_C=80$ Ω and source 100 V rms. Find current, phase, component voltages and power.
questions.answer: $Z=60-j80$ Ω and $\lvert Z\rvert=100$ Ω.::Capacitive impedance is negative imaginary.;;I=1 A rms and $\phi=-53.13^\circ$, so current leads source voltage by 53.13°.::The source voltage phase is measured relative to current.;;$V_R=IR=60$ V and $V_C=IX_C=80$ V.::They are perpendicular phasors, whose resultant is 100 V.;;$P=I^2R=60$ W.::The ideal capacitor has zero mean power.

questions.prompt: An ideal parallel LC has L=0.10 H and C=10 μF, driven at resonance by 10 V rms. Find frequency, branch currents and source current.
questions.answer: $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=1000$ rad/s and $f_0=159.15$ Hz.::Set the input susceptance to zero.;;At resonance $X_L=\omega_0L=100$ Ω and $X_C=1/(\omega_0C)=100$ Ω.::The two reactance magnitudes match.;;$\widetilde I_L=-j0.10$ A and $\widetilde I_C=+j0.10$ A for voltage as reference.::Inductive current lags and capacitive current leads.;;Their sum is zero.::Kirchhoff adds branch current phasors.
questions.final: Branch currents are 0.10 A rms in opposite phase; ideal source current is zero.

questions.target: Series LCR resonance and voltage magnification
questions.prompt: A series circuit has R=10 Ω, L=0.10 H and C=10 μF, with 10 V rms at resonance. Find frequency, current and L/C rms voltages.
questions.answer: $\omega_0=1000$ rad/s and $f_0=159.15$ Hz.::Use the LC resonance formula.;;At resonance Z=R=10 Ω, so I=1 A rms.::Reactive drops cancel at the input.;;Each reactance magnitude is 100 Ω, so $V_L=V_C=100$ V rms.::Multiply branch reactance by the common series current.;;These two voltages are opposite phasors and sum to zero, leaving $V_R=10$ V.::A large internal voltage does not contradict the source voltage.
questions.final: I=1 A; each reactive element carries 100 V rms although the source is 10 V rms.

questions.prompt: A sinusoidal load takes 4 A rms from 230 V rms at power factor 0.75 lagging. Find real power, apparent power and phase angle.
questions.answer: Apparent power is $S_{\rm app}=VI=230(4)=920$ VA.::This is the product of rms magnitudes.;;Real power is $P=VI\cos\phi=920(0.75)=690$ W.::Only the in-phase part contributes on average.;;$\phi=\cos^{-1}(0.75)=41.41^\circ$ with current lagging.::The sign/lead description comes from the supplied power-factor qualifier.
questions.final: P=690 W, apparent power=920 VA, lag angle≈41.41°.

questions.prompt: Derive and compare LR growth/decay and RC charge/discharge, emphasizing initial conditions, time constants and limiting behaviour.
questions.answer: LR obeys $L\dot i+Ri=V$; RC obeys $R\dot q+q/C=V$.::Use Kirchhoff with the element relations.;;Each has form $\dot y=(y_\infty-y)/\tau$ and solution $y=y_\infty+(y_0-y_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}$.::A deviation from steady state decays exponentially.;;For LR, $\tau=L/R$ and $i_\infty=V/R$; for RC, $\tau=RC$ and $q_\infty=CV$.::Compare coefficients.;;Removing the source into a closed discharge path sets the final state to zero, giving $i=I_0e^{-tR/L}$ or $q=q_0e^{-t/RC}$.::Stored energy drives a decaying response.;;Inductor current and capacitor voltage remain continuous at switching under finite drive.::Their derivatives are limited by finite voltage or current.;;During RC charging, current is $V e^{-t/RC}/R$, while charge grows; during LR growth, current itself rises.::Current equals charge derivative only in the capacitor state equation.;;Check t=0, t=∞ and units of τ in every solution.::These three checks catch sign and reciprocal errors.
questions.final: LR time scale is L/R; RC time scale is RC; both are first-order responses with specified initial states.

questions.target: Free versus driven LC and conservation
questions.prompt: Develop free LC oscillation and compare it with an initially uncharged LC circuit subjected to a DC step. Explain energy in both cases.
questions.answer: Free LC gives $L\ddot q+q/C=0$, so for q(0)=q₀ and i(0)=0, $q=q_0\cos\omega_0t$ and $i=-\omega_0q_0\sin\omega_0t$.::The natural frequency is $1/\sqrt{LC}$.;;Substituting into $U=q^2/(2C)+Li^2/2$ gives $U=q_0^2/(2C)$.::Sine and cosine squared sum to one and $L\omega_0^2=1/C$.;;Energy alternates between C and L without loss.::No resistance or external source is present.;;For a DC step the equation is $L\ddot q+q/C=V$, with zero initial q and i.::The source remains connected and changes the forcing.;;The solution is $q=CV(1-\cos\omega_0t)$ and $i=CV\omega_0\sin\omega_0t$.::Shift q by CV and apply initial conditions.;;Now the stored energy changes by source power Vi: $dU/dt=Vi$.::Multiply the circuit equation by i.;;At half a cycle q=2CV, stored energy is $2CV^2$, exactly source work $Vq=2CV^2$; on the return the ideal source can receive energy.::Overshoot is consistent with conservation.
questions.final: Free LC has constant total stored energy; the driven LC step exchanges energy with the source and does not settle.

questions.prompt: Use complex impedance/admittance to explain and contrast series LCR resonance and ideal parallel LC resonance, including current and energy flow.
questions.answer: Series impedance is $Z_s=R+j(\omega L-1/\omega C)$.::Common current permits impedance addition.;;At $\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}$, $Z_s=R$, source current is maximum and in phase, and real power is $V_{\rm rms}^2/R$.::Reactive voltage phasors cancel.;;Individual L and C voltages may greatly exceed source voltage while cancelling each other.::Resonance constrains their sum, not individual values.;;Parallel admittance is $Y_p=j(\omega C-1/\omega L)$.::Common voltage permits admittance addition.;;At the same ideal ω₀, $Y_p=0$ and source current vanishes, while equal opposite branch currents remain.::Reactive current phasors cancel.;;In both cases energy cycles between electric and magnetic stores; a real resistance causes loss and changes ideal sharpness.::Only dissipative elements consume mean power.;;Specify the circuit and its losses before calling resonance “minimum” or “maximum” impedance.::Series and parallel results are opposite.
questions.final: Series resonance minimizes impedance; ideal parallel resonance maximizes it, despite identical ideal LC frequency.

questions.prompt: Derive average power for sinusoidal voltage and current with phase difference, then discuss pure R, L, C and series LCR at resonance.
questions.answer: Let $v=V_0\cos\omega t$ and $i=I_0\cos(\omega t-\phi)$.::φ is the voltage lead over current.;;Use $2\cos A\cos B=\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)$ to obtain $p=(V_0I_0/2)[\cos\phi+\cos(2\omega t-\phi)]$.::Power is the instantaneous product vi.;;Average over a full cycle: the second cosine contributes zero.::It completes an integer number of cycles.;;Since $V_{\rm rms}=V_0/\sqrt2$ and $I_{\rm rms}=I_0/\sqrt2$, $P=V_{\rm rms}I_{\rm rms}\cos\phi$.::Convert peaks to rms values.;;For pure R, φ=0 and P=I²R; for pure L or C, φ=±π/2 and P=0.::Reactive elements return the energy they store in the ideal model.;;At series LCR resonance φ=0, so all input mean power is dissipated in R, although reactive voltages and stored energies are nonzero.::Cancellation of reactances gives unity power factor.
questions.final: Average AC power equals rms voltage × rms current × power factor.
